{
 "repo": "0xMeePok/geth-issue-triage-agent",
 "number": 35726,
 "title": "abigen v2: generated event unpackers skip the decode for an empty payload, returning nil fields with a nil error",
 "body": "#### System information

Geth version: master (abigen v2 codegen)
CL client & version: n/a
OS & Version: Linux
Commit hash : 6c5b3cc35ba3

#### Expected behaviour

For an event that declares non-indexed arguments, `Unpack<Event>Event` returns an error when the log carries no payload, since those fields cannot be filled.

#### Actual behaviour

It returns a nil error and a struct whose non-indexed fields are all nil. Indexed fields are still parsed from the topics, so the result looks valid at the call site.

`accounts/abi/abigen/source2.go.tpl:198` skips the decode instead of attempting it:

```go
out := new({{$contract.Type}}{{.Normalized.Name}})
if len(log.Data) > 0 {
    if err := c.abi.UnpackIntoInterface(out, event, log.Data); err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
}
```

A malformed payload of any other length is reported correctly; only the empty one is silently accepted. Since topic0 is chosen by the emitter, any contract can emit a log with a well-known event topic and no payload, so consumers that read a non-indexed field dereference nil.

  Expected behaviour

  When a peer sends a GetTrieNodes request containing a compact-encoded path longer than 33 bytes, the server should reject or skip it, or even disconnect the peer because it sent a malformed message. A compact-encoded path of 33 bytes represents the maximum trie depth of 64 nibbles (Keccak256 = 32 bytes = 64 nibbles). Any path exceeding 33 bytes is structurally invalid, it cannot address a node in any Ethereum state trie.

  Actual behaviour

  In ServiceGetTrieNodesQuery (eth/protocols/snap/handlers.go), path bytes are passed directly to accTrie.GetNode(accKey), which calls compactToHex(path) (trie/encoding.go) and traverses the trie  without validating the path length.   1. Resource waste: compactToHex allocates a nibble slice of 2*len(path)+1 bytes for every path, then the trie is traversed with this oversized key. A malicious peer could send many requests with  large paths (up to the 10 MB message limit) to amplify memory allocation"
